analysis.one_liner: Lets employers pay disabled adults as young as 18 below minimum wage with fewer safeguards.
analysis.headline: The House Education and Workforce Committee advanced the bill 18-15 on May 21, 2026, and it now awaits a vote by the full House.
analysis.plain_summary: Under a long-standing program, certain employers with a federal certificate may pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage. Since 2014, the law has put limits on this for young workers: anyone 24 or younger had to first receive pre-employment transition services and meet vocational rehabilitation criteria, and every subminimum-wage worker was supposed to get periodic career counseling and referrals to other services from the state. This bill wipes out the young-worker requirements and lets an employer satisfy the counseling rule simply by documenting attempts to contact the state agency, even if the agency never actually provides the counseling.
analysis.who_benefits: Adults with disabilities age 18 and older who want subminimum-wage jobs without first completing transition services or rehabilitation criteria, which the sponsor frames as workplace choice. The employers that hold special wage certificates also gain: they can hire 18-to-24-year-olds directly into below-minimum-wage jobs and keep them there with lighter counseling obligations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Certificate-holding employers and some disabled workers seeking choice

how_it_helps.text: Any employer with a special wage certificate may pay a worker with a disability age 18 or older subminimum wages if the worker chooses the job, replacing the current ban on subminimum work for anyone 24 or younger unless they complete transition services and meet vocational rehabilitation criteria.
Young adults with disabilities can take a certificate-holder job immediately, without first receiving pre-employment transition services or meeting rehabilitation criteria.

The career-counseling requirement is loosened: an employer satisfies it by making documented efforts to contact the designated state agency on the worker's behalf, and the requirement counts as met if the agency then fails to provide the counseling, information, and referrals.
The state agency must make its documentation available to the certificate-holding employer when an individual is employed there.

analysis.who_pays: Young workers with disabilities, who could be placed directly into below-minimum-wage jobs without the transition services, rehabilitation screening, and guaranteed state career counseling that current law requires before or during such work. State vocational rehabilitation agencies also lose their gatekeeping role, since a failed contact attempt by an employer now counts as compliance.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the requirement that workers 24 or younger receive pre-employment transition services and meet vocational rehabilitation criteria before starting subminimum-wage work, allowing them to be placed straight into below-minimum-wage jobs.

It weakens the counseling guarantee: the employer's own documented contact attempts suffice if the state agency fails to respond, so a worker can stay in subminimum work for years without ever receiving career counseling or referrals to jobs at full wages.

The bill concerns the program under which workers with disabilities may lawfully be paid below the federal minimum wage, so any expansion of it increases the number of people working for less than the standard wage floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The choice argument is real: some workers and families value these jobs and resent being forced through rehabilitation steps first, and the sponsor's title frames the bill as restoring employment choice. But the requirements being stripped out were designed to steer young workers with disabilities toward jobs at full minimum wage in mainstream settings. Removing them makes below-minimum pay easier to enter and easier to stay in, and the cost falls on a population with the least bargaining power in the labor market. The employer benefit is concrete and immediate; the worker benefit is the freedom to accept a lower wage.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared committee markup by an 18-15 vote on May 21, 2026 and is waiting for the full House to take it up; no vote has happened yet.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 12, 2026 by Rep. Glenn Grothman with Reps. Wagner and Owens, and referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
On May 21, 2026, the committee held a markup session and ordered the bill reported with amendments by a recorded vote of 18-15.
The bill has not received a vote on the House floor; the 119th Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers holding special wage certificates, whose bill has advanced out of committee. If it stalls, workers with disabilities come out ahead, keeping the transition-services and counseling guardrails that current law places on subminimum-wage employment.

for.name: Rep. Glenn Grothman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to loosen Section 511 restrictions on subminimum wages for adults with disabilities.

for.name: Reps. Ann Wagner and Burgess Owens
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors.

for.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a markup on May 21, 2026 and ordered the bill reported with amendments by an 18-15 vote.

for.name: Providers holding 14(c) special wage certificates
for.role: Disability service providers and workshop operators
for.what_they_did: Have long advocated to preserve and ease the rules of the subminimum wage certificate program their business model depends on.

against.name: 15 House Education and Workforce Committee members
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported, leaving the final committee vote at a narrow 18-15.

against.name: National Federation of the Blind
against.what_they_did: Has long pressed Congress to phase out the subminimum wage program for workers with disabilities rather than expand it.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors are Republicans, and the committee vote was a narrow 18-15; the record does not give the party breakdown of that vote.

industries.industry: Employers holding 14(c) special wage certificates (mostly disability service providers and sheltered workshops)
industries.note: The bill enlarges the pool of workers they can pay below minimum wage and strips the pre-employment services and counseling safeguards that sit between young disabled workers and subminimum jobs. Their gain comes directly out of the wages those workers could otherwise earn at the standard minimum.

The bill sidelines their gatekeeping role: instead of guaranteed counseling and referrals to full-wage jobs, their silence after an employer's documented contact attempts counts as compliance, weakening the pipeline toward competitive integrated employment.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is out of committee but has only five cosponsors and cleared markup by a narrow 18-15 vote, so it needs House leadership to schedule floor time. Contested labor bills that clear committee by slim margins often stall at this stage; the House could still take it up before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, but it would then face the Senate and the White House.
